status: Reviewed authoring proposal; no learner trial, default-branch acceptance or downstream publication claimed.
remainingConditions: Bind actual R2 language/variety/script, checked native materials and a competent assessor; no fixed national pair or cross-role inference.

Require independently pupil-authored actual-R2 poster, invitation and safe written instructions with appropriate information, audience/purpose decisions and revision; drawing, dictation, adult copying or spoken-only instructions do not replace source writing.
Assess the complete informative claim separately: named topic, relevant 2–3 facts and informative drawing/diagram labels; a short source-format product alone does not establish the whole topic.

Retain and separately assess the complete unchanged actual-language oral-rehearsal and sentence-building hard chain. No English word order is imposed, and no native grammar incompatibility is silently resolved.
The complete multimodal candidate and broader R2 writing goal remain withheld; digital/picture-book evidence is not a mandatory source format.

wholeClaim.subject: English
wholeClaim.name: Writing to inform
wholeClaim.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic and supply some information about it
evidence: Write or dictate two or three facts about a familiar topic
Label diagrams or drawings with informative details
Name a topic and provide relevant details about it
wholeClaim.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a few sentences explaining something they know about — like how butterflies grow or how to make a sandwich — naming the topic and sharing some facts?

prerequisiteWholeCards.subject: English
prerequisiteWholeCards.name: Saying Sentences Before Writing Them
prerequisiteWholeCards.description: Say out loud what is going to be written; compose sentences orally before writing them down as preparation for independent writing
evidence: Say a complete sentence aloud before attempting to write it
Rehearse a sentence orally more than once to hold it in memory
Practise sentences with a partner before writing independently
prerequisiteWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts writing a sentence, do they say it out loud first — testing how it sounds — before putting pen to paper?

prerequisiteWholeCards.subject: English
prerequisiteWholeCards.name: Building sentences
prerequisiteWholeCards.description: Understand that words combine to make sentences — a sentence expresses a complete thought; produce and expand complete sentences in speech and writing
evidence: Distinguish between complete sentences and fragments
Compose a complete sentence with a subject and verb
Expand a simple sentence by adding detail
prerequisiteWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says something like "The dog", can they tell you that's not a complete sentence — and add words to make it say something like "The dog ran fast"?

required: Declare actual R2 language/variety/script and competent assessor; do not prescribe a national pair or infer R1 performance as R2 success.
Select/rendition-check actual native written prompts and accepted readings/productions before delivery; English illustrative wording is not a universal assessment script.

Use grammar and sentence/fragment contrasts genuinely valid in that language. Subject+verb does not prescribe English word order; if the full existing card cannot be instantiated, retain the whole-candidate condition as unresolved rather than falsify a contrast.
Record exact pupil writing, audience/purpose choices, supplied support and actual prerequisite performances; copied adult wording or dictated finished sentences are not independent source production.

Keep source-format success, whole informative-topic evidence, whole prerequisite evidence and optional whole multimodal evidence separately scored. Missing material/assessor or an incomplete prerequisite is not a Full result.
bindingContract.schemaBoundary: Strict scoped JSON has no role/material/assessor property. Source identity and public report preserve those conditions; the link is a reusable procedural component, not universal language mastery.

originalPortfolio.sourceDuty: actual-R2 simple poster with appropriate information and purpose
originalPortfolio.givenSituation: Fictional school book exchange, Thursday after lunch in Room A; participants bring one permitted book. A blue curtain is an irrelevant model detail. These are original supplied facts, not a real event announcement.
originalPortfolio.pupilAction: Write an own actual-R2 poster that identifies the event and selects the needed when/where/bring information for pupils. Explain why the curtain fact is omitted. Adult supplies situation facts, not finished wording.
originalPortfolio.wholeInformativeExtension: Use own related actual-R2 sentences giving 2–3 facts about the event, name the topic, and add informative native-script labels to a supplied simple drawing of the room/entry/table. A labelled drawing need not be a scaled map or a digital product.
originalPortfolio.nearMiss: Copied complete adult poster, decorative words without usable event facts, own facts unrelated to the event or adult supplies every written sentence.
originalPortfolio.transfer: Move the event to Room B and change the reader to a younger group; pupil revises relevant information/wording and explains the change.
originalPortfolio.sourceVsWhole: A natural fragment-based source poster may be suitable source writing; it alone does not establish every whole informative/sentence/rehearsal criterion.

originalPortfolio.sourceDuty: actual-R2 invitation with appropriate information and purpose
originalPortfolio.givenSituation: Fictional class craft meeting, Tuesday at ten in the library; invited classmate brings paper; no private address or real recipient contact is needed.
originalPortfolio.pupilAction: Create an own actual-R2 invitation with a welcoming purpose, the correct event/time/place/action information and an appropriate reader-facing form. Explain one information choice.
originalPortfolio.wholeInformativeExtension: Retain own topic and 2–3 relevant written facts; a separate short informative piece can supply whole-topic evidence if a natural invitation uses only labels/fragments.
originalPortfolio.nearMiss: States only that a party exists, omits where/when, copies a supplied invitation or mistakes decoration for useful information.
originalPortfolio.transfer: Change the reader and time; an assessor acting as reader asks a real clarification and the pupil revises a meaningful omission/ambiguity.

originalPortfolio.sourceDuty: actual-R2 simple instructions with appropriate information and purpose
originalPortfolio.givenSituation: Safe paper bookmark task: lay paper flat, fold along the supplied line, then press the crease. No cutting, tools, computer or motor-performance score is required.
originalPortfolio.pupilAction: Write ordered actual-R2 instructions that communicate the safe task to a reader. The reader uses the written words to identify the order and a needed correction.
originalPortfolio.wholeInformativeExtension: Explain the task/topic and supply relevant actual-R2 information; preserve full informative facts/labels evidence separately rather than pretend ordering alone demonstrates every informative criterion.
originalPortfolio.nearMiss: Spoken-only explanation, list of objects with no meaningful order, adult-authored directions or a computer-exactness test substituted for human-readable writing.
originalPortfolio.transfer: Remove one step or change the material layout. Pupil identifies what information is missing and revises the written instructions so the intended reader can act.

sentenceBuilding.actualRoleTask: A competent actual-R2 assessor supplies a genuinely incomplete phrase and complete sentence contrast in that language. Pupil distinguishes them, independently composes a complete grammatical clause with subject and verb, then expands it with a relevant detail. Do not import English ordering or insist a naturally complete nonverbal/elliptical utterance is a fragment.
sentenceBuilding.illustrativeEnglishOnly: If English is the locally declared R2: contrast The club with The club meets; pupil composes an own complete sentence and adds a place/time detail. This is one optional analytic realization, not a national R2 selection or verified other-language translation.
sentenceBuilding.failureBoundary: If the selected language/learner material cannot demonstrate the complete card, retain that limitation; do not soften the edge or credit a label-only product as sentence knowledge.

oralRehearsal.actualRoleTask: Before independently writing an intended actual-R2 sentence, pupil says the intended complete sentence aloud, repeats it to retain it, practises it with a partner and then writes it independently. Record the actual sequence and assistance; speaking after copying is not before-writing rehearsal.
oralRehearsal.failureBoundary: This is the existing whole prerequisite procedure, not an extra NCERT source mandate. Source-only successful written work without this observation does not automatically establish the whole topic/path; do not invent an oral performance.

noMechanicalSoftening.decision: No edge change or necessity counterexample asserted here.
noMechanicalSoftening.why: The sentence card does not specify English order. Written-word/sentence composition is real actual-language competence. An unreported rehearsal is not proof of inability; additional empirical/logical review would be needed before changing method prerequisites.
noMechanicalSoftening.wholePath: All current hard requirements remain, now concretely instantiated and separated from source-only writing evidence.

withheldCandidate.condition: Withheld pending complete source-role/task and remaining claim/dependency compatibility review; the registered historical glossary/note-taking gate has been corrected.
withheldCandidate.currentHardPathInterpretation: Complete remaining hard paths after the registered correction; these paths are not alone a claim that all remaining prerequisites are incompatible.

scoringSeparation.source: Pupil-authored actual-R2 writing in all three formats; select appropriate information for reader and purpose. A naturally brief label/fragment may be source-fit without demonstrating the complete candidate/prerequisites.
scoringSeparation.wholeInformative: Separately demonstrate every informative claim clause, including named topic, relevant facts and informative labels; drawing/dictation permissions in the card do not replace source writing.
scoringSeparation.wholePrerequisites: Separately observe complete actual-language sentence and before-writing oral-rehearsal procedures. Do not infer an unobserved prerequisite from a finished poster.
scoringSeparation.wholeMultimodal: Remains withheld; existing digital/picture-book supplement is unchanged and is not a universal source demand.

card.subject: English
card.name: Making multimodal texts
card.description: Plan, create, edit and publish multimodal texts that combine writing with visual features — images, labelled diagrams, captions, headings and layout — using digital or print tools, choosing visual features to suit the purpose and audience
evidence: Create a digital slide, poster or e-book page that combines a short informative paragraph with a labelled diagram and a caption
Choose images, font sizes and layout in a digital tool to suit a persuasive purpose (e.g. a poster for the school fete) and explain the choices
Publish a picture-book page where the illustration adds meaning not stated in the text, then edit both text and image after feedback
card.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} make a poster or slide that combines writing with pictures, labels and captions — choosing a layout that suits what it's for?

card.subject: English
card.name: Basic Informational Writing
card.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section
evidence: Write an informative text that introduces a topic clearly and groups related information together
Use facts, definitions, and concrete details to develop and explain points about the topic
Provide a concluding statement or section that wraps up the information presented
card.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an explanatory or informative piece — like "How Volcanoes Work" — that introduces the topic clearly, develops it with facts and definitions, and ends with a conclusion?

card.subject: English
card.name: Writing for an audience
card.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organisation are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience, maintaining a consistent style and structure throughout
evidence: Identify the task, purpose, and audience before writing and make deliberate choices about structure, tone, and vocabulary to suit them
Organise ideas logically so that the writing flows from introduction through development to conclusion, with each section serving a clear purpose
Review a draft to check that the organisation, style, and level of formality are consistent and appropriate for the intended reader
card.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes for school, does the piece feel well-organised and appropriate for its purpose — whether it's a formal essay, a creative story, or a persuasive argument — with a consistent tone throughout?

card.subject: English
card.name: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
card.description: Identify the audience for and purpose of writing before beginning, selecting the appropriate form, tone, and register to match the intended reader and communicative goal
evidence: Determine the audience (e.g., peers, teacher, younger children, a public audience) and purpose (to persuade, inform, entertain, or explain) before drafting and explain how these choices affect language and structure
Select an appropriate form for the writing task (letter, report, story, instructions, review) based on audience and purpose
Adjust vocabulary, sentence length, and level of formality to suit the identified audience, e.g. using simpler language for younger readers and more formal language for an official letter
card.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they think about who will read it and why — adjusting their tone, vocabulary, and format accordingly, like writing more formally for a teacher than for a friend?

card.subject: English
card.name: Planning Ideas Before Writing
card.description: Plan before writing by saying aloud or noting down what will be written, writing down ideas and key words, and encapsulating ideas sentence by sentence before composing
evidence: Verbally rehearse sentences before writing them down
Jot key words or ideas in a planning format (e.g., story map) before drafting
Write a simple plan with beginning, middle, and end for a story
card.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they spend a few minutes planning — jotting down ideas, key words, or a rough structure — rather than jumping straight into writing the first sentence?

card.subject: English
card.name: Giving and following instructions
card.description: Use interaction skills to receive and give spoken instructions: listening for each step, asking to clarify, and giving clear, ordered instructions to others
evidence: Follow four spoken instructions in order (e.g. to make a paper aeroplane) and ask a question if a step is unclear
Give a partner clear step-by-step instructions using order words (first, next, then, finally) to draw a simple picture
Check a partner's result and explain which instruction needs changing to be clearer
card.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} three or four steps — like 'get your shoes, then your hat, then wait at the door' — can they follow them in order, and give clear instructions to someone else?

card.subject: Computing
card.name: Step-by-Step Instructions
card.description: Step-by-step instructions for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth); that if instructions are wrong or missing, things go wrong; computers follow instructions exactly
evidence: Write or describe step-by-step instructions for a simple everyday task
Predict what goes wrong if a step is missing or in the wrong order
Explain that a computer follows instructions exactly — it cannot guess what you meant
card.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had to write instructions for making a jam sandwich so precise that even a robot could follow them, could they include every single step?

card.subject: English
card.name: Same purpose, different audience
card.description: Recognise how texts with similar purposes are created differently for different audiences, by comparing word choice, sentence length, images and layout
evidence: Compare two information texts about volcanoes, one for young children and one for adults, and list the differences in words and pictures
Explain how an invitation to a friend's party differs from an invitation to a school assembly for parents
Identify who each of two ads for the same product is aimed at and point to the features that show it
card.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees two ads or books on the same topic — one for little kids and one for grown-ups — can they spot how they're written differently?

remainingUnlinked.meaning: Not26 missing topics. Actual teaching realization still needs language/script material and assessor binding; one precise music meaning remains source-unverified. No all-India/all-board/every-publication completeness claim.

preservation: No canonical claim, guide, prerequisite, age or existing scoped context changes. No Full promotion, fixed R1/R2 pair, learner observation or DB write.
